walkthroughs.title: The Fed's words
steps: The FOMC is the Fed's rate committee. Eight scheduled meetings a year. Put them on your calendar.
It sets a target range, 25 basis points wide, for the fed funds rate: what banks charge each other overnight.
Hawks lean tighter to fight inflation. Doves lean easier to support jobs.
QE means the Fed buys bonds and its balance sheet grows. QT is the reverse.

walkthroughs.title: The data words
steps: CPI is what consumers pay. Core CPI drops food and energy, because those prices swing a lot.
The Fed's 2% inflation goal is measured on PCE, from the BEA. Not CPI.
The jobs report is two surveys. Payrolls come from employers. The unemployment rate comes from households.
GDP is the value of what the economy produces. Real GDP takes inflation out.

walkthroughs.title: The bond words
steps: Bond prices and yields move opposite. Yields up, prices of the bonds already out there go down.
A basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point. A quarter-point Fed move is 25 basis points.
The yield curve lines up Treasury yields from short to long. Normally it slopes up.
Short yields over long ones means it's inverted. That came before each of the last eight recessions, with some false alarms.

questions.q: Which rate is that headline about?
questions.why: The federal funds rate. That's what banks pay to borrow reserves from each other overnight, with no collateral. When you hear the Fed raised rates, that's the one. The Fed doesn't set it to the penny. It sets a target range, here 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and steers fed funds into it with what it pays banks on reserves. Why you care: a move here ripples into other rates, the dollar and credit, and from there into stocks.
questions.lesson_line: When the news says the Fed raised rates, the fed funds target range is what moved.

wrong.SOFR: SOFR is overnight too, but those loans are backed by Treasuries. Fed funds loans aren't, and fed funds is what the Fed targets.
wrong.Interest on reserve balances: That's what the Fed pays banks on their reserves. It's the lever the Fed pulls to steer fed funds, not the headline rate.
wrong.The 3-month T-bill yield: A bill is a loan to the government. Its yield tends to track fed funds, but it isn't the rate the Fed targets.

questions.simple: It's the federal funds rate, what banks charge each other overnight. The Fed sets a range for it.

reasons: fixed before (target range wording)

questions.story: Sept. 16, 2026. The headline on your screen: the Fed raises rates a quarter point, to a range of 3-3/4 to 4 percent.

questions.q: The Fed's Sept. 16, 2026 statement says it hiked in support of its dual mandate. Which two goals is that?
choices: Stable prices and a strong U.S. dollar
Low rates and rising stock prices
questions.why: Maximum employment and stable prices. That's the whole lens. The law actually lists three goals, with moderate long-term rates as the third, but everybody calls it the dual mandate. Notice what's not on the list: the stock market and the dollar. Rate moves hit both, but only as side effects. So the Fed isn't there to hold up your stocks. Read every decision as jobs against prices and you'll know which data it's watching.
questions.lesson_line: Jobs and prices. Read every Fed move through those two.

wrong.Low rates and rising stock prices: Stocks aren't a Fed goal. Rates move stocks, but the job is jobs and prices.
wrong.Price stability, nothing else: That's only half of it. The law puts maximum employment right next to stable prices.
wrong.Stable prices and a strong U.S. dollar: The dollar isn't one of the Fed's goals. Rate moves push it around, but only as a side effect.

questions.simple: Jobs and prices. The law tells the Fed to aim for maximum employment and stable prices, not stock prices.

questions.q: A Fed official on TV gets called a hawk. What's that telling you about how they lean?
choices: Favors tighter policy to curb inflation
Favors easier policy to boost employment
Wants the Fed to buy more bonds
Expects the stock market to fall
questions.answer: Favors tighter policy to curb inflation
questions.why: Tighter policy to curb inflation. A hawk puts inflation first and leans toward higher rates, even if growth and jobs take a hit. The other side of the room is the dove, who leans toward lower rates to support jobs. These are words about Fed policy, not market calls. So when you hear the hawks are gaining ground, think higher rates, not cuts.
questions.lesson_line: Hawk: higher rates, inflation first. Dove: lower rates, jobs first.

wrong.Wants the Fed to buy more bonds: Buying bonds is QE, and QE eases. A hawk leans the other way.
wrong.Expects the stock market to fall: That's a bear. Hawk and dove are about Fed policy, not where the market goes.
wrong.Favors easier policy to boost employment: That's a dove, the other side of the room.

questions.simple: A hawk wants tighter policy and higher rates, because a hawk puts beating inflation ahead of growth.

questions.q: Your econ calendar shows the BLS release that tracks what consumers pay for a basket of goods. Which report is it?
questions.why: CPI, the Consumer Price Index. BLS prices a basket of what consumers buy and tracks how that changes over time. Don't mix it up with the other two price gauges. PPI is the seller's side, what producers get paid. PCE comes from BEA, and it's the one the Fed's 2% goal is written in. You can see CPI day coming in our UCT Terminal: turn on the Macro chip on the calendar and it shows up there, with the estimate and the prior when we have them.
questions.lesson_line: CPI is the shopper's price tag, and BLS puts it out.

wrong.PPI: PPI tracks what producers get paid for their output. That's the seller's side, not the shopper's.
wrong.PCE price index: Close, but PCE comes from BEA, not BLS.
wrong.GDP: GDP measures output, not prices. And BEA puts it out, not BLS.

questions.simple: It's the CPI, the BLS measure of what consumers pay for a basket of goods and services.

reasons: fixed before (PCE wrong-line)

questions.q: What does that number actually count?
choices: Jobs at businesses and in government
People who tell a survey they have a job
New claims filed for jobless benefits
questions.answer: Jobs at businesses and in government
questions.why: Jobs at businesses and in government. Payrolls come from a survey of employers, so they count the jobs on payrolls. Government jobs are in, civilian only. Farm workers, the self-employed and household workers are left out. So the 165,000 is October's change in payroll jobs. I don't try to guess the number. I know it lands that morning, and I watch how the market and my names take it.
questions.lesson_line: Payrolls come from employers. Farm work and self-employment sit outside them.

wrong.People who tell a survey they have a job: That's the household survey, where the unemployment rate comes from. Payrolls come from employers.
wrong.New claims filed for jobless benefits: That's initial claims, a weekly count of people filing for benefits.
wrong.Total hours worked at businesses: The employer survey reports hours too, but the headline counts jobs.

questions.simple: Payrolls count jobs at businesses and in government, as employers report them. Farm work and the self-employed sit outside.
questions.story: Nov. 6, 2026, jobs day. The headline: nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000 in October.

questions.q: What's GDP actually measuring?
choices: Value of final goods and services made
Total spending by the federal government
Total value of the stock market
Money in checking and savings accounts
questions.answer: Value of final goods and services made
questions.why: The value of the final goods and services the country makes. It's the economy's output. Consumer spending, investment, government spending and exports all feed into it. Most of the time the number you hear is a growth rate: how fast real GDP grew from the quarter or year before. So when that report says real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate, that's speed, not size.
questions.lesson_line: GDP is the economy's output. The headline is how fast real GDP grew.

wrong.Total spending by the federal government: Government spending is one piece of GDP, next to consumer spending, investment and exports.
wrong.Total value of the stock market: Stock prices aren't output. GDP counts goods and services made.
wrong.Money in checking and savings accounts: That's part of the money supply, a different measure.

questions.simple: GDP is the value of the final goods and services the country makes. It measures output, not stocks or cash.
questions.story: Oct. 29, 2026: BEA's GDP report for the third quarter is on the calendar.

questions.q: You pull up the Treasury yield curve. What's it showing you?
choices: Yields across maturities, short to long
A single bond's yield over the past year
The gap between stock and bond yields
questions.answer: Yields across maturities, short to long
questions.why: Yields across maturities, short to long. It's one day's picture. Treasury reads it from 1 month all the way out to 30 years, every maturity on one line. That's where you spot an inversion, short yields sitting above long ones. Don't confuse it with a chart of one yield over time. And the Fed's own rate path is the dot plot, a different picture.
questions.lesson_line: The curve is one day, every maturity. One yield over time is a different chart.

wrong.A single bond's yield over the past year: That's the history of one yield. The curve compares many maturities on the same day.
wrong.The Fed's projected rate path: That's the dot plot, the officials' own projections for fed funds.
wrong.The gap between stock and bond yields: That compares stocks with bonds. The curve only compares Treasury yields at different maturities.

questions.simple: The yield curve lines up Treasury yields from short to long maturities on one day, so you can compare them.

questions.q: A strategist on TV says the 10-year moved 25 basis points today. How big is one basis point?
questions.why: 0.01 percentage point. A basis point is one hundredth of a point. So the 25 basis points you just heard is a quarter point. A rate of eight percent is 800 basis points. We use the word because 'up 1%' on a rate can be read two ways. A basis point is always a slice of a point, never a percent of the rate, so nobody misreads it.
questions.lesson_line: 25 basis points is a quarter point. Basis points are slices of a point, never a percent of the rate.

wrong.0.1 percentage point: That's ten basis points, not one.
wrong.1 percentage point: A full point is 100 basis points.
wrong.1% of the current rate: That's a change relative to the rate, and it's exactly the mix-up basis points avoid. They measure the move in the rate itself.

questions.simple: One basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 100 of them make one full point.

questions.q: Someone in chat says the Fed is doing QE again. What does that mean the Fed is doing?
choices: The Fed cutting its target range
The Fed letting its bonds mature
questions.why: Buying bonds on a large scale. Central bankers call it large-scale asset purchases. The Fed buys, its balance sheet grows, and that leans on longer-term rates to push them down. It's not a rate cut. The Fed reached for it when the policy rate was already near zero and it still wanted to ease. QT is the reverse. Lower rates can make stocks more attractive, which is why we pay attention when QE starts or stops.
questions.lesson_line: QE eases by buying bonds. A rate cut eases by lowering the target. Two tools, same direction.

wrong.The Fed cutting its target range: That's a plain rate cut. QE is what the Fed added when the rate was already near zero.
wrong.The Fed letting its bonds mature: That's how QT shrinks the balance sheet, the opposite of QE.
wrong.Congress raising its spending: Government spending isn't a Fed tool. QE is the central bank buying securities.

questions.simple: QE is the Fed buying bonds on a big scale. That grows its balance sheet and pushes long rates down.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The ___ holds eight scheduled meetings a year to set interest rate policy.
questions.why: FOMC. The Federal Open Market Committee holds eight regularly scheduled meetings a year, about one every six weeks. It may also hold unscheduled meetings when developments call for one. A policy statement follows each regular meeting.
questions.lesson_line: The FOMC meets eight times a year on a set schedule, and it can add a meeting when needed.
questions.simple: It is the FOMC, the Fed's rate committee, which holds eight set meetings each year.

reasons: the meeting count is a schedule the FOMC sets and could change

questions.q: What do you call the policy that did that?
questions.why: Quantitative tightening. QT is anything that shrinks the Fed's balance sheet, and $2.2 trillion is a lot of shrinking. This round was mostly runoff: bonds matured and the Fed didn't buy new ones to replace them. Don't mix it up with tapering. A taper only slows new buying, and holdings keep growing until the buying stops. QT comes after that. Think of it as QE run in reverse.
questions.lesson_line: Tapering slows the buying. QT shrinks what's already owned. Two different steps.

wrong.Quantitative easing: QE is the opposite. It buys bonds and grows the balance sheet.
wrong.Tapering its bond purchases: A taper winds down new buying. Until it stops, the Fed is still adding bonds, so holdings still grow.
wrong.Fed forward guidance: Guidance is the Fed talking about future policy. No bonds change hands.

questions.simple: This is QT. The Fed shrinks its pile of bonds by not replacing the ones that mature.

deeper.trap: Tapering and QT are easy to mix up. In November 2021 the Fed announced a phaseout of its asset purchases. That was the taper, and the Fed was still buying. QT comes after buying ends. It shrinks what the Fed already holds, mostly by not replacing bonds that mature.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.story: Chair Powell, October 2025: since June 2022 the Fed's balance sheet has shrunk by $2.2 trillion.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: BLS's index for all items less food and energy is often called ___.
questions.why: Core CPI. BLS publishes an index for all items less food and energy. Some users watch it because food and energy prices are relatively volatile, and they want the core, or underlying, rate of inflation. Headline CPI is all items. Chained CPI and CPI-W are other BLS indexes, not the core.
questions.lesson_line: Headline CPI is everything. Core CPI drops food and energy to show the trend underneath.
questions.simple: It is core CPI, because that index leaves out food and energy, whose prices jump around a lot.

reasons: fixed before ('often called' wording)

questions.q: BEA's PCE price index is on the calendar this week. What does it track?
choices: Prices people pay for goods and services
Prices producers get for their output
The value of goods and services made
What urban consumers pay, per BLS
questions.answer: Prices people pay for goods and services
questions.why: Prices people pay for goods and services. BEA builds it from what people living in the U.S. pay, or what's paid on their behalf. It comes out monthly in the Personal Income and Outlays report. Here's why it matters more than it looks: the Fed's 2% inflation goal is written in PCE, not CPI. So when the Fed talks inflation, that's the scoreboard it's reading.
questions.lesson_line: PCE is the Fed's scoreboard. Its 2% goal is written in PCE.

wrong.Prices producers get for their output: That's PPI from BLS, the seller's side.
wrong.The value of goods and services made: That's GDP. It measures output, not prices.
wrong.What urban consumers pay, per BLS: That's CPI, which BLS builds for urban consumers. PCE is BEA's gauge of what people across the U.S. pay.

questions.simple: PCE tracks what people across the country pay for goods and services. The Fed's 2% goal uses it.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: BLS puts the October 2026 unemployment rate at 4.1%. How is that number built?
choices: Unemployed as a share of the labor force
Unemployed as a share of all adults
People on jobless benefits, as a share
Jobs lost monthly, as a share of jobs
questions.answer: Unemployed as a share of the labor force
questions.why: Unemployed as a share of the labor force. The labor force is everyone working plus everyone unemployed. To count as unemployed you need no job, a job search in the prior 4 weeks, and to be available now. Someone jobless who isn't looking sits outside the labor force, so they're not in the 4.1% at all. Jobless benefits play no part. That's why the rate can drop when people just stop looking.
questions.lesson_line: Jobless and not looking means out of the labor force, and out of the rate.

wrong.Unemployed as a share of all adults: That would count retirees and students. The labor force is only people working or looking.
wrong.People on jobless benefits, as a share: BLS sorts people by their survey answers. Getting benefits has nothing to do with it.
wrong.Jobs lost monthly, as a share of jobs: That's a monthly change. The rate is the share of the labor force out of work at the survey.

questions.simple: It's the jobless people who are looking for work, as a share of everyone working or looking.

reasons: fixed before (temporary-layoff exception)

questions.q: What do you call that shape?
questions.why: Inverted. Short-term yields sitting above long-term ones is the reverse of the normal upward slope. People watch it because inversions have often come before recessions. But it's thrown false alarms too, so it's a warning light, not a sell signal. Steep is the opposite picture, long yields well above short. Flattening is just the gap narrowing, and it can happen with long yields still on top.
questions.lesson_line: Inverted means short above long. A warning light, with false alarms.

wrong.Steep yield curve: Steep means long yields well above short ones. That's the opposite picture.
wrong.Flat yield curve: Flat means short and long are close. Short sitting above long has its own name: inverted.
wrong.Flattening yield curve: Flattening is a move, the gap between short and long narrowing. Long can still be on top. Short above long is inversion.

questions.simple: When short yields sit above long yields, the curve is inverted, the reverse of the usual upward slope.

deeper.trap: Flattening and inverted are easy to mix up. Flattening is the gap between short and long yields narrowing. Inverted means short yields now sit above long ones. The Cleveland Fed says inversions preceded each of the last eight recessions. It also lists false alarms, such as late 2022 through late 2024.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.story: You pull up the Treasury curve and the short end is yielding more than the long end.

questions.q: You see SOFR quoted next to fed funds on a rates screen. What does SOFR measure?
choices: Overnight bank loans with no collateral
The rate the Fed pays on bank reserves
questions.why: Overnight loans backed by Treasuries. SOFR is the cost of borrowing cash overnight with Treasury securities as collateral. The New York Fed publishes it every business day, around 8:00 a.m. ET. Fed funds is overnight too, but those bank loans are unsecured. That's the whole difference: SOFR is secured, fed funds isn't. And only fed funds is the rate the FOMC targets.
questions.lesson_line: SOFR is secured by Treasuries. Fed funds is unsecured. Both are overnight.

wrong.Overnight bank loans with no collateral: That's the fed funds market, and it's unsecured.
wrong.The yield on 10-year Treasury notes: SOFR is an overnight rate, not a 10-year yield.
wrong.The rate the Fed pays on bank reserves: That's interest on reserve balances, and the Fed sets it.

questions.simple: SOFR is the cost of borrowing cash overnight when the loan is backed by Treasury securities.

reasons: edited in the 2026-11-10 variety rewrite

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: BLS's monthly jobs report is titled The ___.
questions.why: Employment Situation. BLS publishes its monthly national job numbers in a news release titled The Employment Situation. It carries the establishment survey's payroll count and the household survey's unemployment rate. Payroll data typically come out on the first Friday of the next month.
questions.lesson_line: On an econ calendar, the jobs report often shows up as Employment Situation. Same report.
questions.simple: BLS calls its monthly jobs report The Employment Situation, and it holds both payrolls and the jobless rate.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: The Fed's Beige Book comes out today. What are you actually going to read in it?
choices: The minutes of each FOMC meeting
The Fed's weekly balance sheet release
questions.why: Reports on local business conditions. Each Reserve Bank talks to directors, business contacts, economists and market experts in its District. The Beige Book collects those stories eight times a year. It's color from the ground, not hard data. Read it for a feel of what businesses are seeing, not for a trade signal.
questions.lesson_line: The Beige Book is stories from businesses, not hard data.

wrong.The minutes of each FOMC meeting: Minutes are their own release, out three weeks after each decision.
wrong.Fed officials' rate projections: Those are in the Summary of Economic Projections, where the dot plot lives.
wrong.The Fed's weekly balance sheet release: That's the H.4.1, the weekly balance sheet, out on Thursdays.

questions.simple: The Beige Book is the Fed's collection of local stories from business contacts, put out eight times a year.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: An FOMC member who leans toward easier policy to support jobs is called a ___.
questions.why: Dove. The Kansas City Fed describes doves as favoring easier monetary policy with an emphasis on maximum employment. Investopedia calls a dove someone who prefers low interest rates. Bull and bear are market words, not Fed policy views.
questions.lesson_line: Doves lean toward cuts, hawks toward hikes. Bulls and bears are about markets, not the Fed.
questions.simple: A dove leans toward easier policy and lower rates, with an emphasis on jobs.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree (Kansas City Fed, Investopedia)

questions.q: When do you get the minutes of that meeting?
choices: The same day as the decision
At the next scheduled FOMC meeting
questions.why: Three weeks after the decision, so the October minutes land in mid-November. Decision day only gives you the statement. The minutes come three weeks later and show the debate behind the vote. Full transcripts wait five years. Put the minutes date on your calendar so a Fed headline that morning doesn't catch you off guard.
questions.lesson_line: Statement on the day, minutes in three weeks, transcripts in five years.

wrong.The same day as the decision: Decision day brings the statement. The minutes come later.
wrong.Five years after the meeting: That's the full transcripts. The minutes come much sooner.
wrong.At the next scheduled FOMC meeting: Meetings are about six weeks apart, and the minutes don't wait. They're out three weeks after the decision.

questions.simple: Minutes come out three weeks after the decision. The policy statement comes out the same day.

reasons: release timing is a Fed practice that could change

questions.story: Oct. 28, 2026: the FOMC holds rates. The policy statement is out the same day.

questions.q: A monster stock rally won't show up in the CPI.
questions.why: True. BLS leaves investment items out of the CPI: stocks, bonds, real estate and life insurance. Those count as savings, not day-to-day spending. So your portfolio can double and the CPI won't notice. It tracks what you pay at the store, not what your assets are worth.
questions.lesson_line: CPI tracks what you spend, not what your stocks are worth.
questions.simple: True. The CPI tracks everyday spending, and stocks and bonds count as savings, so a rally isn't in it.

reasons: fixed before (cost-of-living wording)

questions.q: BLS puts out one price index from the seller's side: what domestic producers get for their output. Which one is it?
questions.why: PPI, the Producer Price Index. It's the seller's side: what producers get paid for what they make. CPI and the PCE price index are the shopper's side, what consumers pay. The Fed tracks PPI along with CPI, so PPI day is one more inflation print on your calendar. When the number hits, know which side of the trade it measures before you read anything into it.
questions.lesson_line: PPI is the seller's side. CPI is the shopper's side. The Fed watches both.

wrong.CPI: CPI is what consumers pay, not what producers get.
wrong.PCE price index: PCE is BEA's consumer price gauge. It's the shopper's side too.
wrong.GDP: GDP is output, not a price index. And it comes from BEA.

questions.simple: PPI tracks the prices producers get for what they make, not what shoppers pay.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: What are initial claims counting?
choices: Repeat filings by people on benefits
New jobs employers added during the week
People who stopped looking for work
questions.why: New applications for jobless benefits. Someone loses a job and files to see if they qualify. That's an initial claim. Continuing claims are the refilings each week after that, from people still on benefits. Claims come out weekly, while the payroll survey is monthly. So between jobs reports, this is your weekly read on layoffs.
questions.lesson_line: Initial claims are first filings. Continuing claims are the refilings. Every Thursday.

wrong.Repeat filings by people on benefits: Those are continuing claims, filed each week someone stays on benefits.
wrong.People who stopped looking for work: They count as out of the labor force. Claims track benefit filings.
wrong.New jobs employers added during the week: Job gains come from the monthly payroll survey, not the weekly claims report.

questions.simple: Initial claims are new filings for jobless benefits by people who just lost a job.

reasons: a release schedule that can change

questions.story: Thursday morning, 8:30 a.m. ET. The weekly jobless claims report hits the wire.

questions.q: The 10-year yield jumps. The price of a 10-year note you already own drops.
questions.why: True. Yields and bond prices sit on a seesaw. When market rates rise, the fixed-rate note you already hold is worth less, so its price falls. That only stings if you sell before maturity. Hold it to the end and you get face value plus interest. It's why yields up and bonds down are the same headline.
questions.lesson_line: Yields up, bond prices down. Think seesaw.
questions.simple: True. Yields and bond prices move in opposite ways, so when yields jump, the note you own is worth less.

reasons: fixed before (narrowed to fixed-rate Treasuries)

questions.q: A macro account posts that M2 is growing again. What is M2 measuring?
questions.why: A broad measure of the money supply. M2 is M1 plus small time deposits and retail money market fund shares. Think of it as money people can spend, or park for a short time in something safe. The Fed reports it in its H.6 release. It's not the Fed's bond pile, and it's not new cash printed. When you hear M2, think cash and deposits across the economy.
questions.lesson_line: M2 is money to spend or park short term: M1 plus small time deposits and retail money funds.

wrong.Total Fed holdings of bonds: That's the Fed's securities pile. It grows with QE and shrinks with QT.
wrong.New cash printed this year: M2 isn't new cash. It's M1 plus small time deposits and retail money fund shares.
wrong.Bank loans to small businesses: Loans are credit. M2 counts money: cash, deposits and money fund balances.

questions.simple: M2 measures money: the safe assets people can spend or hold as short-term investments.

reasons: fixed before (securities holdings wording)

questions.q: When the Fed set rates at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, it named a range 25 basis points wide, not one exact rate.
questions.why: True. The Fed names a range, never one number. 3-3/4 to 4 percent is 25 basis points wide, and it's been set that way since December 2008. It held there at the October meeting. A hike lifts the whole range and a cut drops it. So 'the Fed is at 4' is shorthand. The real setting is the whole range.
questions.lesson_line: The Fed sets a range 25 basis points wide. A hike moves the whole range.
questions.simple: True. The Fed names a range a quarter point wide, not one exact rate.

reasons: a policy setting that changes over time (the range shown is dated)

questions.q: It's a June FOMC day and the Fed puts out its projections. Where do you see each official's call for the rate at year-end?
questions.why: The dot plot. Each dot is one official's view of where the midpoint of the fed funds range should be, at each year-end and over the longer run. They're views, not promises, and the Fed itself says they carry a lot of uncertainty. The market mostly watches the median dot. That's the number to note on a projection day.
questions.lesson_line: Dots are views, not promises. Watch the median dot.

wrong.The yield curve: The curve shows market yields by maturity, not what officials think.
wrong.The Beige Book: The Beige Book is stories on local business conditions.
wrong.CME FedWatch: FedWatch is CME's tool. It shows the odds of a Fed move priced by traders, not the officials' own views.

questions.simple: It's the dot plot. Each dot shows one Fed official's view of where the rate should be.

deeper.trap: FedWatch and the dot plot measure different things. FedWatch tracks the odds of a change to the Fed rate. The dot plot shows what officials themselves project. It is also not known which dot belongs to which official, so you cannot read one person's view off the chart.

reasons: fixed before (sentence length)

questions.story: Inflation has cooled and hiring has slowed. At its meeting, the FOMC lowers its target range for the federal funds rate.
questions.q: What's the Fed doing here?
questions.why: Easing. Cutting the fed funds target eases policy. Cheaper loans pull more spending into the economy, and lower rates can make stocks more attractive too. Raising rates is the opposite, tightening. Tapering is about slowing bond buying, not the rate. And disinflation is the backdrop in your story, slower price gains, not something the Fed did.
questions.lesson_line: Cuts ease. Hikes tighten.

wrong.Tightening: Tightening is raising rates to cool demand and inflation. This was a cut.
wrong.Tapering: Tapering is slowing bond buying. This was a rate cut.
wrong.Disinflation: That's what prices did, rising more slowly. It's the backdrop, not what the Fed did.

questions.simple: Cutting the rate target is easing. Lower rates are meant to get people spending.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Someone quotes the inflation rate for everything in the basket, food and gas included. What's that number called?
questions.why: Headline inflation. It's the whole basket, food and energy included. Those two swing a lot, so headline jumps around. Core takes them out so you can see the trend underneath. Here's the twist: the Fed's goal uses headline PCE, not core. So don't write off a hot headline as just gas prices.
questions.lesson_line: Headline is the whole basket. Core is the trend underneath.

wrong.Disinflation: Disinflation is inflation slowing down, with prices still rising.
wrong.Core inflation rate: Core leaves food and energy out, so it isn't everything.

questions.simple: Headline inflation counts every item, food and energy too. That's why it jumps around more than core.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: A headline says disinflation is here. What's actually happening to prices?
choices: Food and energy taken out of CPI
questions.why: Prices are still rising, just more slowly. That's disinflation. Nothing got cheaper on average. Falling prices is deflation, a different animal. BLS uses December 2023 to December 2024 as its example: consumer prices rose, but by less than before. So when you hear disinflation, think the inflation rate is cooling, not that your groceries got cheaper.
questions.lesson_line: Disinflation is not deflation. Prices still go up, only slower.

wrong.Prices falling across the economy: That's deflation, prices falling over time.
wrong.Prices rising faster each month: That's inflation speeding up, the opposite of disinflation.
wrong.Food and energy taken out of CPI: That's core CPI, a narrower index.

questions.simple: Disinflation means prices still go up, just more slowly than before. It's not falling prices.

deeper.trap: A falling inflation rate still means a rising price level. Mix up disinflation and deflation and you misread the whole report.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: BEA says real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter. What makes it real?
choices: It's final, with no more revisions
It's measured in that period's prices
questions.why: It's adjusted to remove inflation. Real, or chained, GDP takes price changes out so one period compares fairly with another. Nominal GDP uses each period's own prices, so some of its growth is just prices going up. That's why the 3.4% you hear is real growth. And real has nothing to do with revisions. BEA estimates every quarter three times.
questions.lesson_line: Real means after inflation. The GDP growth you hear is real growth.

wrong.It's final, with no more revisions: Real has nothing to do with revisions. BEA estimates each quarter three times.
wrong.It's measured in that period's prices: That's nominal GDP, in current dollars.
wrong.It counts only physical goods: GDP counts services too, not just goods.

questions.simple: Real GDP has price changes taken out, so different years can be compared fairly.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The Fed raised its range by 1/4 percentage point, or 25 ___.
questions.why: Basis points. One basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 1/4 percentage point is 25 of them. Investor.gov's example: eight percent is 800 basis points.
questions.lesson_line: Fed statements say percentage points. Traders say basis points. A quarter point is 25 bps.
questions.simple: A quarter of a percentage point is 25 basis points, since one basis point is a hundredth of a point.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Late 2021, the headlines say the Fed is starting to taper. What's it doing?
choices: Slow and then end Fed bond buying
Sell bonds the Fed already owns
Cut the fed funds rate in steps
Raise the fed funds rate slowly
questions.answer: Slow and then end Fed bond buying
questions.why: Slowing its bond buying, then ending it. In November 2021 the Fed announced it would phase out its purchases. In December it doubled the pace, with buying set to end by mid-March 2022. A taper doesn't shrink what the Fed owns. It just adds less each month until it stops. Shrinking the pile is QT, and that came later. Watch the words too: in 2013 a hint of a taper alone sent yields spiking.
questions.lesson_line: Taper is QE winding down, not QT. The Fed stops adding before it starts shrinking.

wrong.Sell bonds the Fed already owns: A taper doesn't touch what the Fed owns. Shrinking that is QT, a later step.
wrong.Cut the fed funds rate in steps: Tapering is about bond buying, not the rate.
wrong.Raise the fed funds rate slowly: Rate hikes are a separate tool. A taper only slows the bond buying.

questions.simple: Taper means the Fed slows its bond buying step by step until it stops, without selling what it owns.

reasons: fixed before (QT wrong-line)

questions.q: You want PCE day marked on your calendar. Which BEA report do you look for?
questions.why: Personal Income and Outlays. BEA puts the PCE price index and core PCE in that monthly report. The title doesn't say PCE, which is how people miss it. The jobs report is BLS's Employment Situation, and PPI is its own BLS release. Learn the name and you won't get surprised by the Fed's favorite inflation number.
questions.lesson_line: Personal Income and Outlays on the calendar means PCE day.

wrong.Producer Price Index: PPI is its own BLS release, about what producers get paid.
wrong.Summary of Economic Projections: That's the Fed's projections, four times a year at FOMC meetings.

questions.simple: PCE comes out each month in BEA's Personal Income and Outlays report, along with core PCE.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Each FOMC decision is voted on by the 12 Reserve Bank presidents.
questions.why: False. All 12 presidents sit in and join the debate, but only five vote at a time. The 12 votes belong to the seven Board governors, the New York Fed president and four of the other eleven presidents, on a rotation. The rotation turns over at the first meeting of the year. So when you read a dissent, check whether that person actually votes this year.
questions.lesson_line: Twelve votes: seven governors and five presidents. The rotation changes each year, so check who votes.
questions.simple: False. All 12 presidents sit in and talk, but only five of them vote at any one time.

deeper.trap: A president without a vote is not out of the debate. Nonvoting presidents attend, join the discussion and help shape the Committee's view of the economy and policy options. Only the vote count needs this year's list of members.

reasons: fixed before (sentence length)

questions.q: The Fed statement says it expects to keep rates low for a long time. What's that kind of message called?
questions.why: Forward guidance. It's the Fed telling you how it expects to set policy down the road. Words, not a purchase. And it works: when the FOMC used explicit guidance, expected short rates and long-term bond yields fell. Long rates price what the market expects the Fed to do, not just today's rate. So read the statement's language, not just the decision.
questions.lesson_line: Forward guidance is words about future policy. Read the language, not just the decision.

wrong.The Beige Book: That's the stories on local business conditions.
wrong.Quantitative easing: QE is buying bonds, an action, not a statement about the future.
wrong.The dual mandate: That's the Fed's goals: maximum employment and stable prices.

questions.simple: Forward guidance is the Fed saying how it expects to set policy. Yields fell when the FOMC used it.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: There are eight FOMC meetings a year. Which ones come with fresh projections and a new dot plot?
choices: Every one of the eight meetings
Only when the Fed changes rates
questions.why: March, June, September and December. Every governor and every Reserve Bank president turns in projections four times a year, at those meetings. The charts come out right after the meeting ends. The other four meetings bring no new dots. Mark those four on your calendar. They're the meetings where you get the Fed's outlook, not just its decision.
questions.lesson_line: Four of the eight meetings bring new dots: March, June, September, December.

wrong.Every one of the eight meetings: Eight meetings, but only four rounds of projections.
wrong.Only the year-end December meeting: December is one of four. March, June and September bring them too.
wrong.Only when the Fed changes rates: Projections run on a fixed schedule, four times a year, move or no move.

questions.simple: New projections and a new dot plot come at four meetings a year: March, June, September and December.

reasons: the projection schedule is a Fed practice that could change

questions.q: The 10-year went from 5.24% on Oct. 1, 2026 to 4.94% on Oct. 30. How many basis points did it fall?
questions.why: 30 basis points. 5.24 minus 4.94 is 0.30 of a percentage point. A basis point is a hundredth of a point, so 0.30 times 100 is 30. Say it that way and nobody hears a 30% drop. The yield fell 30 hundredths of a point, not 30% of itself.
questions.lesson_line: Quote yield moves in basis points. It kills the percent-of-a-percent mix-up.
questions.simple: It fell 30 basis points. Each hundredth of a percentage point is one basis point.

deeper.trap: Do not call this a 30% drop. The yield fell 30 hundredths of a percentage point. Percent talk about a rate is easy to misread. Basis points remove the doubt: they measure the change in the rate itself.

reasons: computed key

wrong.0.3 basis points: You stopped at 0.30 and never turned it into hundredths.
wrong.1,018 basis points: You added the two yields instead of subtracting.
wrong.300 basis points: One decimal place off. 0.30 of a point is 30 basis points.

questions.q: Month to month, headline inflation swings more than core.
questions.why: True. Headline counts everything, food and energy included, and those prices swing hard. A Fed governor called headline measures inherently noisy. Core strips food and energy out so you can see the trend underneath. So when one month's headline looks wild, check core before you decide inflation has turned.
questions.lesson_line: A wild month in headline is often gas or groceries. Check core first.
questions.simple: True. Headline counts food and energy, whose prices jump a lot, so it moves around more than core.

reasons: fixed before (attribution)

questions.q: Jobs day. The payroll number and the unemployment rate come in the same report. Where does the payroll number come from?
questions.why: The establishment survey. The jobs report runs on two surveys. The establishment survey asks employers, so it counts jobs on payrolls, plus hours and earnings by industry. The household survey asks people, and that's where the unemployment rate comes from. Two surveys, two different questions. That's how payrolls and the jobless rate can tell different stories in the same report.
questions.lesson_line: Payrolls from employers, jobless rate from households. Two surveys, one report.

wrong.Household survey: The household survey asks people. That's where the unemployment rate comes from.
wrong.Weekly jobless claims: Claims are a separate weekly release about benefit filings.
wrong.The Fed's Beige Book: That's the Fed's stories from business contacts. No payroll count, and it isn't part of the jobs report.

questions.simple: The payroll count comes from the survey of employers. The survey of homes gives the jobless rate.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: BEA's advance GDP estimate is the final number for that quarter.
questions.why: False. BEA estimates each quarter three times. The advance estimate lands about a month after the quarter ends, and it's an early look. The second and third estimates add data that wasn't in yet. So treat the first print as a first draft. It can change after the market has already reacted to it.
questions.lesson_line: The first GDP print is a first draft. Expect revisions.
questions.simple: False. The advance estimate is BEA's first look, and two later estimates add more data.

deeper.trap: The advance estimate is an early look, built on the best information available at the time. BEA's second and third estimates add source data that were not available a month earlier. Treat the first print as a first draft.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: A $250,000 time deposit at a bank counts in M2.
questions.why: False. M2 only picks up small time deposits, the ones issued under $100,000. At $250,000 this one is well over that line, so it sits outside M2. It's a narrow detail, but it shows what M2 is built from: money people can spend or park for a short time.
questions.lesson_line: M2 counts small time deposits only, under $100,000.
questions.simple: False. M2 only counts time deposits under $100,000, so a $250,000 one is left out.

reasons: one cited fact only

questions.q: A Treasury on your screen matures in 20 years. What kind is it?
questions.why: A Treasury bond. Bonds are the long end, 20 or 30 years. Notes run 2, 3, 5, 7 or 10 years, so no note goes out 20. Bills are a year or less, and floating rate notes run two years. So when people say the 10-year, that's a note. The 20 and the 30 are bonds.
questions.lesson_line: Bills are short, notes run up to 10 years, bonds are 20 or 30.

wrong.A T-bill: Bills are short-term, a year or less.
wrong.A Treasury FRN: Floating rate notes mature in two years, so a 20-year can't be one.
wrong.A T-note: Notes stop at 10 years. A 20-year Treasury is a bond.

questions.simple: It's a Treasury bond. Bonds run 20 or 30 years, and notes stop at 10.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.story: Dana's job ended for good in the spring. She'd like work but hasn't looked in two months. BLS surveys her household.
questions.q: How does BLS count her?
questions.why: Not in the labor force. To be unemployed you need three things: no job, a search in the prior 4 weeks, and being available. Dana hasn't looked in two months, so she misses the search test. Wanting work isn't enough. The one exception is a temporary layoff with a recall expected, and her job ended for good. That's how the unemployment rate can miss people who've stopped looking.
questions.lesson_line: Wanting work isn't enough. BLS asks if you looked in the prior 4 weeks.

wrong.Employed between jobs: She has no job, so she isn't employed.
wrong.Unemployed, on layoff: The layoff exception is for workers expecting a recall. Dana's job ended for good.
wrong.Unemployed, she wants work: Wanting work doesn't count. She hasn't looked in the prior 4 weeks, so she misses the test.

questions.simple: She's not in the labor force, because she hasn't looked for work in the last 4 weeks.

deeper.counter: Change one fact. Dana is on a temporary layoff and expects her employer to call her back. Now BLS counts her as unemployed, even though she has not looked for work. Expecting a recall replaces the job search test.

reasons: fixed before (layoff exception)

questions.story: The fed funds rate is already near zero. The economy still needs help. The Fed starts buying huge amounts of longer-term Treasuries.
questions.q: What do you call this move?
questions.why: Quantitative easing. The rate can't go much lower, so the Fed buys bonds instead. With the policy rate near zero, the FOMC ran large-scale purchase programs to push longer-term rates down. That's QE, and it grows the balance sheet. After the financial crisis the Fed bought roughly $3.7 trillion over six years. Lower long rates can make stocks more attractive, which is why we watch QE closely.
questions.lesson_line: When the rate can't go lower, the Fed can still buy bonds. That's QE.

wrong.Quantitative tightening: QT shrinks the balance sheet. Buying bonds grows it.
wrong.Forward guidance: Guidance is talk about future policy. Here the Fed is buying bonds.
wrong.Cutting the rate target: The rate's already near zero. Buying longer-term Treasuries is a different tool, QE.

questions.simple: Buying lots of long-term bonds when the rate is already near zero is QE, quantitative easing.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.story: Treasury yields on Oct. 30, 2026: 3-month 4.16%, 2-year 4.56%, 10-year 4.94%, 30-year 5.31%.
questions.q: What shape is the curve, and what's it telling you?
questions.why: Sloping up, the usual shape. Read it left to right: 4.16% at 3 months, 4.56% at 2 years, 4.94% at 10, 5.31% at 30. Longer money pays more. That's the normal case, because longer maturities only sometimes yield less. A curve sloping up isn't the recession warning. Inversion is, and this curve isn't inverted.
questions.lesson_line: Read the curve left to right. Yields rising with maturity is the normal shape.

wrong.Inverted, short yields on top: Inverted needs short yields above long ones. Here the 3-month is the lowest of the four.
wrong.Sloping up, a recession warning: Right shape, wrong read. A recession has seldom followed a steep, upward curve within two years.
wrong.Inverted, a recession warning: Inversions have come before recessions, but this curve isn't inverted. The 3-month, at 4.16%, is the lowest yield here.

questions.simple: It slopes up, the usual shape. Each longer maturity pays more, from 4.16% up to 5.31%.

deeper.trap: Four points can hide a kink. On Oct. 30 the 20-year yielded 5.34%, a bit above the 30-year at 5.31%. A curve can slope up overall and still dip at one spot. Read every maturity before you name the shape.

reasons: fixed before (flat wrong-line)

questions.q: CME FedWatch shows strong odds of a cut at the next meeting. Where do those odds come from?
questions.why: Fed funds futures prices. FedWatch backs the odds out of 30-Day Fed Funds futures. So it's what traders are betting, not what the Fed has decided. The dot plot is the officials' own view, and the vote only happens at the meeting. When FedWatch and the dots disagree, the market and the Fed see the path differently. That's worth knowing before a Fed day.
questions.lesson_line: FedWatch is the market's bet, not the Fed's plan. Compare it with the dots.

wrong.Votes cast by FOMC members: Votes happen at the meeting. FedWatch odds are priced before it, from futures.
wrong.A survey of economists: No survey. The odds come out of futures prices.
wrong.The Fed's dot plot: The dots are officials' projections. FedWatch is what traders are pricing.

questions.simple: FedWatch odds come from fed funds futures prices, so they show what traders expect, not what the Fed plans.

reasons: the key rests on one cited fact (CME's FedWatch page)
CME's page timed out on re-check 2026-11-12, so the quote was not re-confirmed

questions.story: Over the past year, the overall price level fell. A basket of goods that cost $1.00 now costs $0.98.
questions.q: What's going on with prices here?
questions.why: Deflation. Prices fell. A basket that cost $1.00 a year ago costs $0.98 now, prices down about 2% on the year. That's BLS's own example. Disinflation is different: prices still rise, just slower. Mix the two up and you misread the whole report.
questions.lesson_line: Deflation means prices fall. Disinflation means they rise slower.

wrong.Disinflation: Disinflation is prices still rising, just more slowly. Here they fell.
wrong.Recession: A recession is a broad drop in economic activity. Your story is about prices.
wrong.Tightening: Tightening is the Fed raising rates. Your story is prices themselves falling.

questions.simple: Prices fell, so this is deflation. Disinflation would mean prices still rising, just more slowly.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.story: Oct. 28, 2026: the FOMC held its range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. Two voters dissented. They wanted a 1/4-point hike.
questions.q: How would you label the two dissenters?
questions.why: Hawks. The room held at 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and these two wanted a 1/4-point hike. That's a vote for tighter policy, inflation first. The statement itself said inflation remains elevated. Read the dissents every meeting. They show you which way the debate inside the room is leaning.
questions.lesson_line: A dissent for a hike is a hawkish vote. Read the dissents.

wrong.Doves: Doves lean toward easier policy. These two wanted a hike.
wrong.Bears: Bears are pessimists about markets. This is about Fed policy.
wrong.Bulls: Wanting a higher rate isn't a market call. Bulls and bears are market words. Hawks and doves are Fed words.

questions.simple: They're hawks. They wanted a rate hike when the majority voted to hold.

questions.story: September 2026 CPI: all items up 0.6% for the month. Gasoline jumped 9.1%, over half the rise. Core rose 0.3%.
questions.q: Why did headline run hotter than core?
choices: Core is measured over a year
questions.why: Energy, which core leaves out. Gasoline jumped 9.1% and drove over half of the 0.6% headline rise. Core is all items less food and energy, so the gas spike never touched it, and core rose 0.3%. Both are monthly numbers. Shelter stays in core, and core has services as well as goods. On CPI morning that's the first thing I want to know: broad, or just gas.
questions.lesson_line: When headline and core split, look at energy and food first.

wrong.Shelter, which core leaves out: Shelter stays in core. Only food and energy come out.
wrong.Core counts only goods: Core has services too. Airline fares and medical care were among September's increases.
wrong.Core is measured over a year: Both are monthly. Core was up 0.3% in September, the same span as the 0.6% headline.

questions.simple: Gas prices drove it. Core leaves out energy, so the gas jump lifted headline but not core.

reasons: fixed before (causal wording)

questions.story: September 2026, versus a year earlier: CPI up 3.7%. PCE price index up 3.6%. Core PCE up 3.1%.
questions.q: Which number is the Fed's 2% goal written in?
questions.why: PCE, up 3.6%. The Fed's goal is 2% a year, measured by the annual change in the PCE price index. That's headline PCE, food and energy in. The Fed leans on core PCE to read the trend, and it watches CPI too, but the goal itself is written in PCE. Look at all three here. Whichever you pick, inflation is running well above where the Fed wants it.
questions.lesson_line: Goal in PCE, trend in core PCE.

wrong.CPI, up 3.7%: The Fed watches CPI, but its 2% goal is written in PCE.
wrong.Core PCE, up 3.1%: Core PCE helps the Fed read the trend. The goal itself uses the full PCE index.
wrong.PCE, last month: The goal is 2% a year, the annual change in PCE, not one month's move.

questions.simple: It's PCE. The Fed's 2% goal is measured by the yearly change in the full PCE price index.

deeper.trap: The trap is core. The Fed often relies on core PCE to identify underlying trends. But a Fed governor put it plainly: controlling headline inflation, not core, is the ultimate aim. Here headline PCE was 3.6% and core 3.1%, both well above 2%.

reasons: a stated policy goal the FOMC can revise

questions.story: BEA's advance estimate: real GDP grew at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter of 2026.
questions.q: How much did real GDP grow inside the quarter itself?
questions.why: About 0.8%. BEA quotes quarterly GDP at an annual rate unless it says otherwise. That's the pace the quarter would hit if it ran for a full year. So 3.4% annualized is about 0.8% for the quarter, and BEA prints both in the same release. Read the label before you react to the number.
questions.lesson_line: GDP headlines are annualized. Check which rate you're reading.

wrong.About 13.6%: You stretched it the wrong way. The 3.4% is already a full-year pace.
wrong.About 3.4%: That's the annualized pace, not the quarter's own growth.
wrong.Can't tell: You can. An annual rate stretches the quarter over a year, so the quarter's own growth is much smaller. Only 0.8% fits.

questions.simple: About 0.8%. The 3.4% is a yearly pace, and one quarter on its own grows much less.

deeper.trap: Read the label, not just the number. BEA's release prints 3.4 percent at an annual rate and 0.8 percent at a quarterly rate, side by side.

reasons: fixed before (lesson shortcut removed)

questions.story: October 2026: nonfarm payrolls rose by 165,000. A friend says that means 165,000 more people have jobs.
questions.q: What's your friend missing?
questions.why: Payrolls count jobs, not people. Someone on two payrolls gets counted at each one. Head counts come from the household survey instead. So the 165,000 is October's change in payroll jobs. It isn't 165,000 more people working. Close, but not the same thing.
questions.lesson_line: Payrolls count jobs. The household survey counts people.

wrong.Payrolls count only part-time work: Payrolls count full- and part-time workers who got paid.
wrong.That's the count of unemployed: BLS counted 7.1 million unemployed that month. The 165,000 is the change in jobs.
wrong.Payrolls count only private firms: Government jobs are in there too, civilian ones.

questions.simple: Payrolls count jobs, not people, so someone on two payrolls is counted at each one.

deeper.trap: A person on two payrolls is counted at each one. So the job count can rise without more people working. People are counted by the household survey, which produces the unemployment rate.

reasons: archived release numbers; definitions from the BLS CES FAQ

questions.story: During October 2026 the 10-year Treasury yield fell from 5.24% to 4.94%. You bought a 10-year note on Oct. 1.
questions.q: What happened to your note's price?
questions.why: It rose. Yields fell from 5.24% to 4.94%, and when yields fall, the price of a fixed-rate note already out there goes up. Your interest payments don't change, they're fixed. Before maturity the price floats above or below face value. Hold it to the end and you get face value plus interest either way.
questions.lesson_line: Falling yields are rising bond prices. Same move, two ways of saying it.

wrong.It fell: That's what happens when yields rise. Here they fell.
wrong.It stayed at face value: A note pays face value at maturity. Before then its price moves with rates.
wrong.Its interest payments fell: The payments on a fixed-rate note are set. Falling yields move its price, not its interest.

questions.simple: When yields fall, prices of bonds already issued go up, so the note's price rose.

deeper.trap: Yield and price are two views of one move. On Oct. 1, 2026 the 10-year yielded 5.24%. By Oct. 30 it yielded 4.94%. A note bought on Oct. 1 still pays the same fixed interest, but its market price rose as yields fell. Held to maturity, it returns face value plus interest either way.

reasons: stable definition; several Tier 1 or agreeing Tier 2 facts

questions.q: Two straight quarters of falling real GDP is the NBER's definition of a recession.
questions.why: False. The NBER calls a recession a significant decline in activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months. Deep, wide and lasting. Most recessions it has dated did include two down quarters of real GDP, but not all of them. 2001 didn't. So two quarters is a shortcut people use, not the definition.
questions.lesson_line: Two down quarters is a shortcut. The NBER looks at depth, breadth and length.
questions.simple: False. The NBER looks for a deep, wide, lasting drop, and the 2001 recession had no two down quarters in a row.

reasons: fixed before ('official' wording)

questions.q: A Reserve Bank president without a vote this year doesn't get a dot on the dot plot.
questions.why: False. Every governor and every Reserve Bank president turns in a projection, voter or not. So there are more dots than votes. The dots carry no names, so you can't tell whose is whose. That's one more reason we watch the median, not any one dot.
questions.lesson_line: The dot plot shows every participant, not just the voters.
questions.simple: False. Every governor and every Reserve Bank president adds a dot, voter or not, and no dot has a name.

deeper.trap: Only 12 members vote at a meeting, but every governor and every Reserve Bank president submits a projection. So the dot plot holds more views than there are voters. The dots carry no names, so you cannot pick out this year's voters. Markets mostly watch the median dot.

reasons: question text edited in the 2026-11-10 variety rewrite

questions.q: From 2022 the Fed shrank its balance sheet, mostly by selling the bonds it owned into the market.
questions.why: False. It was mostly runoff. The May 2022 plan shrank holdings by reinvesting less of the money from maturing bonds, under monthly caps. For Treasuries the cap started at $30 billion a month and rose to $60 billion. No fire sale. The bonds just matured and weren't replaced. Quiet, but it's still tightening.
questions.lesson_line: That QT was mostly runoff. No fire sale.
questions.simple: False. The Fed mostly let its bonds mature and didn't replace them, rather than selling them.

deeper.trap: Runoff is quiet, but it is still tightening. QT means policies that reduce the size of the Fed's balance sheet, and letting bonds mature without replacing them did exactly that. Chair Powell said the balance sheet shrank by $2.2 trillion since June 2022.

reasons: fixed before (runoff wording)

questions.story: 2013: the Fed chair hints the Fed may soon slow its bond buying. Treasury yields spike and markets turn volatile.
questions.q: What did the market end up calling it?
questions.why: The taper tantrum. In 2013 Chair Bernanke hinted the Fed might soon slow its bond buying. Treasury yields spiked and markets got volatile. The Fed hadn't even slowed yet. Its last QE round didn't end until October 2014, and QT only started in October 2017. The lesson for us: the market trades the Fed's words before its actions.
questions.lesson_line: The market trades the Fed's words before its actions.

wrong.Quantitative tightening: QT didn't start until October 2017. In 2013 the Fed was still buying.
wrong.A yield curve inversion: Yields spiked. Inversion means short yields above long ones, a different thing.
wrong.The rate-hike scare: The hint was about slowing bond buying, not raising the rate. That's why it got the taper name.

questions.simple: It was the taper tantrum. A hint of slower Fed bond buying sent Treasury yields spiking.

deeper.trap: The tantrum came from words, not action. The Fed was still buying bonds in 2013. Its last QE round ended in October 2014, and it began shrinking its holdings only in October 2017. A hint about slowing purchases was enough to send Treasury yields up.

reasons: Tier 1 Board speech footnote, re-fetched 2026-11-12

questions.q: The yield curve has inverted before without a recession following.
questions.why: True. It's a warning light, not a sure thing. Inversions came before each of the last eight recessions. But late 1966 and late 2022 through late 2024 were false alarms, and a very flat curve in late 1998 was another. The rule of thumb says a recession about a year after an inversion. Read it with caution, and don't use it to time your trades.
questions.lesson_line: An inversion is a warning light, not a sure thing.
questions.simple: True. Inversions led the last eight recessions, but 1966 and 2022 to 2024 were false alarms.

deeper.counter: An FDIC study lists more misses: the 1966 inversion, near-inversions in 1987 and 1995, and the 1998 inversion. It also says the curve can flatten or invert for reasons that do not foreshadow slower growth.

reasons: a track record that changes as new data arrive

questions.story: The economy peaked in December 2007. The NBER announced that peak on December 1, 2008.
questions.q: What does that tell you about waiting for the NBER?
choices: It comes long after the turn
It comes within days of the turn
It comes with the next GDP report
questions.answer: It comes long after the turn
questions.why: It comes long after the turn. The peak was December 2007. The NBER named it December 1, 2008, 12 months later. That's how they work: they wait until the evidence is clear, and their calls have come four to 21 months after the turn. By then it's old news. Don't wait on an official call to manage risk. Your stops and the price action tell you far sooner.
questions.lesson_line: Don't wait for the NBER to manage risk. Its call comes months late.

wrong.It comes within days of the turn: The quickest call on record still took four months.
wrong.It comes with the next GDP report: It's slower than that. Here it took 12 months.
wrong.It forecasts the next turn: The NBER doesn't forecast. It names a peak months after it happened.

questions.simple: The NBER names a turn long after it happens, here 12 months later. Its call is old news.

deeper.example: The fastest call on record still came four months late, after the February 2020 peak. The slowest took 21 months. Even at its quickest, the turn was old by the time it was named.

reasons: fixed before ('official' wording)

questions.story: A loan rate goes from 10% to 11%. One headline says the rate rose 10%. Another says it rose 1%.
questions.q: Which way of saying it can't be misread?
questions.why: Up by 100 basis points. Up 10% could mean the rate is now 11% or 20%, depending on how you read it. Up 1% leaves people guessing what the 1% is a share of. A 100 basis point move takes a 10% rate to 11%, no doubt about it. One basis point is a hundredth of a percentage point, so 100 of them is one full point.
questions.lesson_line: Say rate moves in basis points or percentage points, never in percent.

wrong.Up 10% in a headline: That's a percent of the old rate. Some readers will think the rate is now 20%.
wrong.Up 1% in a headline: One percent of what? Read as a share of the old rate, it's barely a move.
wrong.Up by 10 basis points: Too small. Ten basis points is a tenth of a point. From 10% to 11% is 100.

questions.simple: Saying 100 basis points can't be misread. Saying 10% or 1% leaves people guessing what you meant.

deeper.example: Same move, three ways. From 10% to 11% is 1 percentage point, or 100 basis points. Saying it rose 10% is a percent of the old rate, and some readers will take it as 20%. Saying it rose 1% leaves readers asking: 1% of what? Basis points name the move itself.

reasons: fixed before: the right choice was lengthened on 2026-11-11

questions.q: Oct. 30, 2026: the 2-year Treasury yields 4.56%, the 10-year 4.94%. What is the 10-year minus 2-year spread?
questions.why: 38 basis points. The spread is the 10-year minus the 2-year. 4.94 minus 4.56 is 0.38 of a point. Times 100, that's 38 basis points. Positive means the curve still slopes up from 2 to 10 years. If it drops below zero, that part of the curve is inverted. It's the spread I check first when someone says the curve is inverting.
questions.lesson_line: Track the 10-year minus 2-year in basis points. Below zero, that stretch is inverted.
questions.simple: The spread is 38 basis points, because the 10-year yield sat that far above the 2-year.

deeper.trap: Order matters. FRED subtracts the 2-year from the 10-year. Flip it and the sign turns negative, which reads like an inverted curve when it is not.

reasons: computed key

wrong.-38 basis points: You subtracted in the wrong order, the 10-year from the 2-year.
wrong.0.38 basis points: You stopped at 0.38 and never turned it into hundredths.
wrong.950 basis points: You added the two yields instead of subtracting.

questions.q: When the FOMC meets, SOFR is the rate it sets.
questions.why: False. The FOMC sets a target range for the federal funds rate. SOFR is a market measure: the cost of borrowing cash overnight against Treasuries. The New York Fed publishes it every business day, not just on Fed days. So on Fed day, the number you're waiting for is the fed funds range.
questions.lesson_line: The FOMC sets the fed funds range. SOFR is a daily market rate.
questions.simple: False. The FOMC sets a range for the fed funds rate, while SOFR is a daily measure of secured borrowing costs.

deeper.trap: The FOMC's decision is a target range for the federal funds rate, not SOFR. The New York Fed publishes SOFR every business day, not only on meeting days.
